JZ for the seventieth birthday — Hans Huber, “Einige Bemerkungen über die Rechts- und Staatslehre von Carl Schmitt. Zu Peter Schneiders Buch ‘Ausnahmezustand und Norm’.” In: Juristenzeitung 13, 1958, pp. 341–343.

1959 JZ — Adolf Schüle, “Eine Festschrift.” In: Juristenzeitung 14, 1959, pp. 729–731. See also the resulting letters-to-the-editor debate in Deutsche Zeitung of 24 February, 22 March, and 23 March 1960.
1962 NZZ — H. F. Pfenninger, “Carl Schmitt und der ‘Partisan’ Rousseau.” In: Neue Zürcher Zeitung, 27 July 1962.
indocilis privata loqui — “Unable to speak like an ordinary mortal.”
Et mortem sentire juvat — “It is a comfort to feel death approaching.” Pharsalia, IV, 570.
princeps reliogissimus Sisebut — Correctly: religiosissimus, “the most devout King Sisebut.” Sisebut (died 621) was king of the Visigoths.
Lecto de la validez and the validez del Lecto — “Reading validity” and “the validity of the reading.”
Vitoria later dealt with it in exactly the same way — In his Relecciones de Indis, Francisco de Vitoria rejects forced baptism.

Coactus voluit — Etsi coactus tamen voluit, “although compelled, he nevertheless willed it.” A formula of Roman contract law according to which agreements entered into under compulsion were still valid, although their validity could be challenged.
Innocent III and his decretal Maiores — Innocent III, pope from 1198 to 1216, ruled that a forced baptism was invalid.

Canon 57 of the Fourth Council of Toledo and Gratian’s gloss, C 5 D. XLV — The Fourth Council of Toledo, held in 633 under the presidency of Isidore of Seville, condemned the forced baptisms of Jews ordered by King Sisebut. This was incorporated into the Decretum Gratiani, Chapter V, Distinction XLV.
À corsaire, corsaire et demi — A French proverb meaning that an aggressive person must be met by someone even more aggressive.

Secundum occasionem et veritatem coactus sive condicionaliter, sive absolute voluit — “According to the circumstances and the truth of the matter, though compelled, he willed it either conditionally or absolutely.”

Quevedo’s Sueños — Schmitt is referring to Francisco de Quevedo, Los sueños, Buenos Aires 1952. A copy with annotations is in his papers, RW 265 no. 22688; German: Die Träume, Frankfurt am Main 1980. Also: idem, La hora de todos y la fortuna con seso, Madrid 1987.

The latter work, published posthumously, incorporated “La isla de los Monopantos.” On its relationship to the Protocols of the Elders of Zion, see J. A. van Praag, “Los ‘Protocolos de los Sabios de Sión’ y la ‘Isla de los Monopantos’.” In: Bulletin Hispanique 51, 1949, pp. 169–173.
Through gentleness—practice this duty … — Schmitt is remembering lines from a hymnbook here; see BW EJ, p. 354.
as Ernst Jünger said against me — BW EJ, p. 247. See also above, pp. 222 f.
Pribićević — Svetozar P. (1875–1936), Croatian-Serbian politician who initially supported a united Yugoslavia, but from 1927 onward adopted the opposite position and went into exile in 1931.

Sava told me — Sava Kličkovič (1916–1990), Serbian, a student of Schmitt in Berlin from 1936 and awarded his doctorate in 1940. See Christian Tilitzki, “Carl Schmitt – Staatsrechtler in Berlin. Einblicke in seinen Wirkungskreis anhand der Fakultätsakten 1934–1944.” In: Etappe 7, 1991, pp. 95 f. Schmitt remained on friendly terms with Kličković and his family throughout his life. An extensive correspondence survives in his papers.
It is most dangerous with Bonald — Louis-Gabriel-Ambroise, vicomte de Bonald (1754–1840), French counter-revolutionary philosopher who “sociologized the idea of God” (R. Spaemann).
Crooke — Possibly a reference to John Crook, Consilium Principis. Imperial Councils and Counsellors from Augustus to Diocletian, Cambridge 1955.
Jünger’s new diary — E. Jünger, Jahre der Okkupation, Stuttgart 1958. On Niekisch, see the note above on p. 79.
ready or not to go, he must stand before his judge — F. Schiller, Wilhelm Tell, end of Act IV.
Henry Morgenthau — (1891–1967), U.S. Secretary of the Treasury from 1934 to 1945, originator of the “Morgenthau Plan,” which proposed turning Germany into an agricultural state.
“out of regard …” — After initially accepting the Nobel Prize, Boris Pasternak declined it on 29 October 1958 under massive pressure, explaining that he did so:
“out of regard for the society in which I live.”
ERP funds — From 1948 onward, funds from the European Recovery Program, based on the Marshall Plan, were made available to support economic reconstruction.
Montherlant’s Maître de Santiago — Henry de Montherlant, Le Maître de Santiago, play, 1947; German: Der Ordensmeister, 1948.
Hans-Joachim Arndt — (1923–2004), political scientist, a member of the Heidelberg circle of Schmitt’s informal students; see van Laak, passim.

leyenda negra — Faced with the accusation that they were a brutal people, Spaniards answered with the term leyenda negra—“Black Legend”—coined in the late nineteenth century, which presented the accusation as anti-Spanish propaganda.
sublime néant — In Montherlant’s Le Maître de Santiago, the character Alvaro wavers between God and the “sublime nothingness.”

journalist Cassandra — The cover story in the issue of Der Spiegel mentioned here concerns the English journalist William Neil Connor (1909–1967), who wrote columns for the Daily Mirror for more than thirty years under the pseudonym Cassandra. In the interview with Der Spiegel, he emphasizes his contempt for everything German.
if the Germans are not what he says they are—what is he? — A variation on The Education of Henry Adams; see the note above on p. 136.
Erich Strauss — Schmitt occasionally published poems under the pseudonym Erich Strauss; see Gedichte.
In 1932 I found the decisive word — This refers to LuL.
I wrote to Jünger that I already feel embarrassed enough —

“Niekisch belongs to the victors of the Second World War, and he already made my wife feel that in 1946. As far as I am concerned, he can go on winning and write history as a victor. I will not answer the lies he spreads about conversations with me. It is embarrassing enough for me that I ever entered into a conversation with him at all, when thirty years later I am presented with this kind of ‘report’ by him about that conversation.”
BW EJ, pp. 356 f. See also the note above on p. 79.
Steppenverhöre — Allusion to Werner Helwig, Das Steppenverhör. Roman, Düsseldorf/Cologne 1957.
doceo, sed frustra — “I teach, but in vain”; see the note above on p. 180.

Haecker’s afterword of 1918 — This refers to Haecker’s afterword to his 1917 edition of Kierkegaard’s Begriff des Auserwählten, which was also published separately by Hegner in Hellerau in 1918; now in idem, Essays, Munich 1958, pp. 9–87. See the note above on p. 110.
preacher’s tabs exchanged for a rosary — This refers to Haecker’s conversion from Protestantism to Catholicism.
“The Last Day will not be a single day, but simply that period which is also called the thousand-year kingdom.”

“abyss of mendacity of degenerate Furche pietists” — T. Haecker, Essays, Munich 1958, p. 81. “Furche pietists” refers to authors associated with the Furche publishing house, founded in 1916, which had an explicitly Christian program.
You can no longer think of anything to say about Hitler — An allusion to the anti-Hitler writer Karl Kraus, who remarked in 1933:
“As for Hitler, nothing occurs to me.”
The story of the three men — W. Helwig, Das Steppenverhör; see the note above on p. 377.
letter from October 1923 — A letter from Feuchtwanger to Schmitt, not from October but from 18 June 1923; in: BW Feuchtwanger, pp. 35 f.
“jument ruant étalon” — The Baldung Grien engraving is correctly titled: “Étalon et la jument Kicking avec des chevaux sauvages.”

Our venerable head of state … — Federal President Heuss’s speech was printed in the FAZ of 17 December 1958. A copy with underlining and stenographic notes survives in Schmitt’s papers, RW 265 no. 20830. See also BW Mohler, pp. 293 f.
Obiter dictum and obiter factum — “Something said in passing” and “something done in passing.” In legal practice, an obiter dictum is an opinion expressed by a judge apart from the judgment itself.

the reading of Odo Marquard’s study — Schmitt is referring to Odo Marquard, Skeptische Methode im Blick auf Kant (Symposion, 4), Freiburg im Breisgau/Munich 1958. A copy containing many annotations and inserted newspaper clippings survives in Schmitt’s papers, RW 265 no. 27763.
I do not compare the victims; I compare only the judges — A reversal of a sentence by Lucien Laberthonnière; see the note above on p. 214.
Rafo Konforti — A character in Ivo Andrić’s novel Das Fräulein, which appeared in German in 1958.
chorus in Nestroy’s farce Judith — Correctly:
“We Hebrews have miracles enough in our history; We can do without miracles of bravery.”
Quid sum miser tunc dicturus? / Quem jutorem rogaturus? — Correctly: Quid sum miser tunc dicturus? / Quem patronum rogaturus?
“What shall I, poor wretch, say then? What advocate shall I ask for?”
Quotation from the hymn Dies irae. Schmitt replaces patronum—“advocate”—with jutorem—“helper.”
my thesis about the transformation of the subject matter of a trial — See above, p. 42. Schmitt published nothing further on this. Compare his remark from 1958:
“A fundamental scholarly investigation is needed into the question of how far the means and methods of a judicial process alter the very object that the process is supposed to examine.”
judex homini lupus — “The judge is a wolf to man.”

J’en appelle de ta justice à ta réalité — Actually: J’en appelle de ta justice à ta gloire, meaning: “I appeal from Your justice to Your glory.” Léon Bloy, Das Heil und die Armut. Mit Beiträgen von Georges Bernanos, Raïssa Maritain und Karl Pfleger, Heidelberg, 1953, p. 374. In his diary, Léon Bloy records that Ernest Hello said this sentence to him (entry of 13 August 1892). He later uses it in his description of the Last Judgment in Chapter 28 of his book Le Salut par les Juifs. Schmitt names Hello as his source; cf. RK, pp. 55–56.
My tables — Shakespeare, Hamlet, Act I, Scene 5: “My tables, — meet it is I set it down.” Schlegel translates this into German as: “Writing tablet, here! I must write it down.”
μὴ μνησικακεῖν — not to keep the wrongs one has suffered in mind; not to bear a grudge.

JW Jan. 1933 — Dr. Ernst Wichards, Regional Court Councillor at the Prussian Ministry of Justice, “Das Reichsgesetz über Straffreiheit vom 20. Dezember 1932.” In: Juristische Wochenschrift, issue 1, 62nd year (1932), appendix.

Duguit — Léon Duguit/Henry Monnier, Les constitutions et les principales lois politiques de la France depuis 1789. Collationnées sur les Textes Offic., précédées de Notices Histor. et suivies d’une Table Analyt. détaillée, Paris, 1898.

Jean de Saint-Thomas — Schmitt quotes him from Charles Journet, L’Église du Verbe incarné, Paris, 1941 and later editions. In the Fribourg 1962 edition, the passage that Schmitt quotes somewhat inaccurately appears on pp. 875–876.
Bellarmin — Roberto Bellarmino, De Summo Pontifice, Ingolstadt [1587].
Billot — Ludovico Billot, Tractatus de ecclesia Christi sive continuatio theologiae de verbo incarnato, Rome, 1909.
Ed. Meyer — Eduard Meyer, Caesars Monarchie und das Principat des Pompejus. Innere Geschichte Roms von 66 bis 44 v. Chr., Stuttgart/Berlin, 1918 and later editions.

pomerium — “the strip of open ground left free along the city wall, both inside and outside it, marked off by stones and defining the limits of the city’s auspices; the open space around the wall” (Georges, Latin-German dictionary).

Procul e [correctly: a] muris … — “Then, outside the walls and some distance away, a detachment appeared. It was not advancing in scattered little groups, but in an ordered formation, as if marching against an enemy of equal strength. They advance at a run …”
Michelet, la loi; the Vistula as a border — See the note above on p. 20.
1901. Education of Henry Adams — See the note above on p. 136.
